item.title: Coefficient Giving: Reflecting on our Recent Effective Careers RFP
item.description:
Published on August 28, 2026 12:19 AM GMT

Reflections from the Effective Giving & Careers team.

 

Earlier this year we ran our first open call for the effective careers side of our work — a request for proposals from organizations that help people move into high-impact careers. We’re excited to share the results: We’re awarding $13,075,301 in grants to 28 organizations via the Effective Giving & Careers Fund, and several other Coefficient Giving funds expect to fund up to 16 more.

That ~$13 million is well above the ~$5 million we originally estimated, which reflects both the volume and the quality of applications. The RFP drew 474 applications. From that pool, 111 organizations advanced to a more in-depth second-stage review, either with us or with a partner team. Weighting each grant’s modeled social return on investment by its funding amount gives a mean of roughly 5,500x — though these are early, uncertain estimates.

Who’s receiving funding

These are some of the organizations that were awarded grants, grouped by their primary function (although most of them do more than one thing). Each grant works to transition more people into high-social-impact work across cause areas like global health and economic development, farm animal welfare, global catastrophic risks, and climate, and each takes a rigorous approach to using evidence, reasoning, and cost-effectiveness analysis in aiding these transitions.

Fellowships and structured placements:

  • School for Moral Ambition (University Fellowship): An undergraduate fellowship that helps place students at high-impact organizations, anchored by a paid summer placement
  • World Bank Government Analytics Fellowship: A hybrid fellowship that trains government managers and analysts, primarily in low- and middle-income countries, to use data to improve real policy and reform decisions in their own institutions
  • Johns Hopkins PAVE: A vaccine-training program that places graduate students into internships at global health institutions such as WHO, Gavi, UNICEF, and PAHO
  • University of York (Thanzi Studentships): Funds African professionals to complete a remote, part-time M.Sc. in Health Economics at the University of York’s Centre for Health Economics
  • CEGA (Center for Effective Global Action) Global Networks Fellowship: A UC Berkeley talent program for scholars from sub-Saharan Africa, now adding a policy track for people in or moving toward government, think-tank, and policy-institution roles
  • Health Progress Hub: Connects qualified professionals in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia with evidence-based global health organizations that are looking to hire, through recruitment support and fellowship tracks
  • ODI Fellowship: ODI places early-career economists into government institutions across low- and middle-income countries; this grant supports an effort to measure the program’s long-term career and institutional impact

Incubators and accelerators:

  • The Agency Fund: Embeds senior technical talent into Global South nonprofits to build their data and technology capacity, while moving experienced technologists into impact-focused work
  • LabSocial: A Latin America–based incubator that trains mid-career professionals to design and launch cost-effective new organizations; this grant supports its scale-up, including an expansion into Brazil and new social for-profit and policy entrepreneurship work
  • Kickstarting for Good: An incubator, funded to run an accelerator for early-stage high-impact organizations and a podcast recruiting entrepreneurial talent

Talent-matching and career advising:

  • Escape the City (Impact Matching Platform and Podcast): A long-running U.K. career-change platform for mid-to-senior professionals from consulting, finance, and tech — building tools and programs to connect them with high-impact roles
  • Pivot to Good: A new initiative helping mid-to-senior corporate professionals move into high-impact careers through a podcast and a professional network that routes candidates to established programs
  • Tech Safari (Building Back Home program): Channels African diaspora professionals toward high-impact work on the continent through a community, a podcast, and a curated jobs board
  • Jewish Social Impact (JSI): Channels American Jews toward higher-impact careers and giving through a fellowship, one-on-one advising, and writing
  • Scale Wise: Brings experienced mid-career professionals into impact-first roles and advises organizations scaling their work across Africa and Asia
  • Netherlands Effective Environmentalism Initiative: Advises aspiring climate professionals toward the most neglected, high-leverage areas of climate work, and helps other career advisors do the same
  • South Asian Effective Careers: An India-based careers platform offering high-quality one-on-one advising and mapping high-impact organizations across the region

Media and advocacy: 

  • Government Works: A newsletter and jobs resource for careers in government and public service, with an editorial focus on state-capacity and systems-change work
  • Who Let the Docs Out: Supports impact-documentary filmmakers with production grants and mentorship; this grant funds a student track focused on animal-protection topics
  • Class Action Network: Advocacy and organizing grant working to increase visibility of high-impact career paths

Competitions:

  • The Giving Pitch: A university pitch competition in which students compete to recommend grants to effective charities, designed to introduce finance- and consulting-track students to high-impact philanthropy
  • Hack the Fork: Runs hackathons at elite institutions that incubate alternative-protein projects and surface talent for animal welfare work

The most common grants were to EA-affiliated career advising programs and high-impact fellowship programs in Sweden, France, Israel, Norway, Estonia, and Poland. These were explicitly evaluated by how many high-impact career transitions could be facilitated per unit of budget cost, and measured against our bar.

What we funded, and what we learned

A few patterns stand out. While EA-affiliated career advising programs are the most common by count, most of the total funding went to fellowships and structured placements. Incubators and accelerators account for a meaningful share, and the rest spans media, coaching, competitions, and one advocacy grant. 

Of the 28 grants, 13 are cause-neutral, supporting high-impact transitions across our priority areas. The other 15 overlap strongly with one or two specific cause areas, with global health and development the heaviest concentration. We set out to focus on mid-career and senior professionals (much existing infrastructure skews toward students), and on LMIC talent pipelines, where many high-impact organizations operate but career infrastructure remains thin. The bigger surprise was about the ecosystem itself. We estimated a 25% chance we’d receive more than 40 applications; we got almost 500. We also came in assuming we’d fund far fewer proposals and give away considerably less money.

This indicates that we systematically underestimated both the size and the quality of the effective-careers space. We also mispredicted its shape: We expected most fundable applications to look like EA career-transition programs, and while we did receive many of those, many of the strongest opportunities came from impact-focused organizations well outside the EA network — several of which were not previously on our radar. 

Based on our cost-effectiveness estimates for about 85% of the recommended grants, weighted by funding, every dollar invested is expected to create about $5,500 of social benefit. (Read more on our framework for calculating social return on investment.) The numbers look strong, but they are early and uncertain. Relatedly, we saw a wide range of how applicants monitor their outcomes, and we’re considering an internal project to help set and share clearer standards. 

Looking ahead

We are considering another Effective Careers RFP next year. For a future call, we’d cast a wider net — promoting through development, policy, public health, and academic channels. We may consider a dedicated incubation/acceleration track and a small-grants track for nascent efforts. 

As always, the credit belongs to the organizations doing the work. We’re grateful to everyone who applied, and we’ll aim to share more as we learn how these grants play out.

item.title: Is mild lifelong acne really worse than stunted growth?
item.description:
Published on August 27, 2026 10:54 PM GMT

A preliminary estimate, and a request for better ones.

Summary

I believe the standard literature estimates for the number of DALYs attributable to a case of stunting are too low, largely because they don’t account for the long term effects. This means that childhood nutritional interventions that reduce the prevalence of stunting may be substantially more cost-effective than previously believed.

Epistemic status

Exploratory and back-of-envelope, ~100 hours invested in an area well outside my expertise. I have moderate-to-low confidence in any single point estimate, but high confidence that the standard literature value of 0.23 DALYs greatly underestimates the lifetime burden of stunting. I’m posting this to be red-teamed. If you have a better method, or know of data I’m missing, please let me know.

AI use

I’ve had many conversations with Claude about this topic, and used Claude to develop the ideas, find references, and help generate the accompanying model. I’ve also previously discussed the topic with Grok, Gemini, and ChatGPT, all in their respective research / long-answer modes. The text of this post is all mine.

Conflict of interest

This post is written in my professional capacity at Semilla Nueva, an organization that makes more nutritious corn. As such, I am biased towards thinking that malnutrition is a big deal. For what it’s worth though, I already thought malnutrition was a big deal - more specifically “one of the largest scale and most tractable causes of human suffering and lost potential for flourishing” - long before I started working at Semilla Nueva.


Why should we care?

Humans need a good diet to grow. Not just enough calories, but a long list of other macro and micro nutrients, including quality protein and minerals like iron and zinc. When those are missing, a child can fail to reach their genetic potential. That outcome is called stunting.[1] Stunting has been common throughout human history. It became rare in rich countries only in the last couple of centuries, and these days affects about 22% of children under five years of age worldwide. Since stunting is permanent[2], it affects a similar proportion of adults, actually somewhat higher since their critical early-growth period took place when stunting prevalence was higher.

Malnutrition serious enough to interfere with growth causes a lot of other problems along the way. It weakens immune function, raises the risk of chronic disease, and, at least on the maternal side, raises the risk that the next generation is stunted too. The same improvement in nutrition that made stunting rare in rich countries is probably part of what drove the Flynn effect[3], because the poor nutrition behind stunting also impairs cognition and lowers wages. As countries continue to develop, the prevalence of stunting will likely continue to decline.

Improving children’s diets to reduce stunting looks straightforwardly good. Stunting is also an unusually convenient thing to measure compared to other effects of an improved childhood diet. Immune function is hard to measure at population scale, IQ is fraught to measure at population scale, but height is trivial to measure and is already being measured ~everywhere. So reduction in stunting, or acceleration of growth, has become a standard outcome for dietary interventions: give some number of children a nutritional supplement, and a fraction of them will shift from below the stunting threshold to above it. There are many studies on the topic. Quantifying total global philanthropic spending is difficult, but my best guess is that about 3-5% of global health funding goes into childhood nutritional interventions[4].

To bring that outcome into the standard EA framework, we need one more number: how many disability adjusted life years (DALYs) should you attribute to one case of stunting? That, alongside org-specific numbers on costs and reach, makes it possible to calculate DALYs per dollar. There is a widely-used value, but it looks surprisingly low: with 3% discounting, 0.23 DALYs per case[5], justified in the source with nothing more than “from the assumption.” I emailed the first author of that paper, and he replied that he no longer stands by that estimate, but declined to give me an updated one. For comparison, all using 3% discounting, clubfoot is generally estimated at 7.4 DALYs, lifelong moderate iron deficiency anemia[6] or lifelong Kwashiorkor (moderate wasting with edema) is 1.5 DALYs[7]. GBD stopped discounting future DALYs in 2010 and I generally think that’s the right accounting, but include both discounted and undiscounted figures here to enable comparison.

My own current best guess is that the average moderate or severe[8] case of childhood stunting costs on the order of 2.3 DALYs[9] (subjective 80% confidence interval 1.2 - 4.2)[10]. This estimate comes from starting with the Years of Life Lost (YLLs) from stunting, then estimating the Years Lived with Disability (YLDs) by comparing stunting to similar conditions that already have disability weights (like mild acne or anemia) and multiplying that weight by how many years the person is expected to live afterward.

Background on DALYs and GBD (feel free to skip if those are familiar acronyms)
The Global Burden of Disease study is a pillar of the global health and development world; GBD 1990 was the first serious attempt to quantify global disease, and invented the concept of DALYs. The core idea can be summarized in one line: disability-adjusted life years equal years of life lost plus years lived with disability (DALYs = YLL + YLD). YLL is relatively simple, comparing the age someone actually dies with their life expectancy. YLD relies on a disability weight (DW) from 0 (perfect health) to 1 (death) multiplied by the duration of disability. Older GBD versions set these DWs by expert judgment; newer ones essentially poll people on which health state they’d prefer[11] and convert the answers into a weight. Moderate acne, for instance, has a DW of 0.067, meaning that state is treated as about 93% as good as perfect health. A disability weight for stunting existed in GBD 1990[12], but has been removed and has not been added back[13].

YLL Component

There’s an excellent new GBD paper on total costs of child growth failure, which computed the total annual DALY burden of stunting on children under age 5 at 33 million per year, basically all as YLLs[14] - stunted children are more likely to die young due to disease. It’s not that stunting causes increased disease death per se, just that the same nutritional deficiencies that lead to stunting also lead to reduced immune function. Specifically, about 23% come from increased risk of death from diarrheal disease[15], 52% from increased risk of death from lower respiratory infections[16], 13.5% from increased risk of death from malaria[17], and 11% from increased risk of death from measles[18]. Combining that with the fact that about 132.5 million children are born per year[19] and that 22.3% of children are stunted, we can calculate stunted children, on average, lose 1.1 DALYs[20] during their first 5 years of life[21]. However, that GBD paper is making the unusual decision of including mild cases of stunting (height for age Z score or HAZ < -1), whereas most literature only includes moderate and severe stunting - so just naively dividing them uses too large a numerator. To address this, I model attributable burden across the HAZ distribution, and estimate that 59% of the burden comes from HAZ < -2 (Tabs E and F of the model), i.e. moderate and severe stunting, which brings YLLs to 0.66. In practice, this comes out to a bit under 1% of stunted children dying before age 5. The lack of accounting for any long-term effects like reduced cognitive function makes sense given that stunting doesn’t have any disability weight. 

YLD Component

If a stunted child survives, how might we quantify the disability state of being stunted? Without running the massive surveys GBD uses to establish the DWs, the best I can do is to consider various other health states, anchoring on some that seem worse and some that seem better, with the goal of triangulating in on a DW. This of course involves some judgement calls, which is why I wanted to do the thinking in public and invite other perspectives. It’s widely accepted that stunting (or more precisely the nutritional deficiencies that lead to it) has long-term effects on cognition, but the standard GBD framework doesn’t account for the long-term effects because it’s challenging to do well[22].

To make that comparison, I excerpted 27 (of about 2100) rows of the health sequelae DW table from GBD 2019, choosing conditions either related to stunting and malnutrition or to things I feel able to imagine, like acne or hair loss. I’m including 8 here, with more in the “DW Comparison” tab of the model.

Intellectual disability

Stunted people have lower wages - perhaps somewhat due to the stunting itself via the same effects that cause a wage return to people in the middle of the height distribution in rich countries and due to reduced capacity for physical labor from the smaller body frame, but almost certainly primarily due to cognitive impairment not caused by stunting but caused by the same childhood malnutrition that caused the stunting. Many papers and press releases simply state that stunted people have lower wages by 10-20% compared to people of similar SES who are not stunted. Victora et al found that 1 Z-score of height is associated with an 8% increase in wage[23], which I use in the model (Tab D). This means that an average case of moderate stunting implies a 12% reduction in wage, whereas the average severe case implies a 21% reduction[24]. In light of this information, my best guess is that the average case of stunting is associated with intellectual losses roughly equivalent to the average borderline intellectual functioning[25] - though of course the cognitive effects of malnutrition, like the height effects, vary significantly in severity. Following GBD convention, I’m not including lost wages as a health effect, so the direct DALY contribution from wage is 0, and is instead used to help inform my reasoning about how bad the cognitive effects are through other quality of life pathways.

Table 1: Some conditions one might compare stunting to to assess YLDs.

Upper and lower anchors

In estimation and forecasting, I often find it helpful to also establish bounds that I’m confident the true value must lie between - depending on how the remainder of the process goes, these can either comprise the final uncertainty interval, or can be a broader superset of the plausible range of values.


Lower anchor: Moderate and severe stunting cause intellectual disability that seems roughly equivalent to the GBD health state “borderline intellectual function”, in addition to all the other sequelae of stunting like shorter stature, reduced physical strength, and higher probability of having offspring below a healthy weight range. As such, I’m happy to take that DW of 0.011 as a lower anchor[26]. Multiplied through low-SES in the developing world life expectancy of 67 years[27], we get 0.74 YLDs as the floor. The same math applies for lifelong mild alopecia areata (spotty hair loss) or mild acne. To account for the possibility that this judgement is wrong and mild acne is in fact worse, I applied a further 25% haircut, expanding the bottom of the CI down to 0.55.


Upper anchor: Severe wasting is an acute state of near-starvation, and never sustained long - people either recover or die. It’s definitely a worse state than being stunted. Moderate anemia is also almost certainly worse, and comes in at 3.5 YLDs if sustained for life, which I think is a good upper bound for at least moderate stunting. To account for the possibility that moderate anemia is actually less bad than stunting, the upper edge of the CI is a bit higher, at 4. For more comparisons, see Tab B of the model.

Table 2: Headline estimates

Conclusion

Stunting is definitely bad, and hopefully something that will continue to become rarer during the coming decades. Stunting kills a bit under 1% of those it afflicts before the age of 5, which puts the average YLLs for a case of stunting at 0.66. Those who survive have some level of mild ill-health throughout the remainder of their lives, a combination of shorter stature, reduced strength, and a mild cognitive impairment. Weighing the YLDs of those sequelae is challenging and imprecise, but my best guess from modeling the major effects at various levels of stunting gives a population-weighted average for moderate and severe stunting of 1.6. Combining the YLLs and YLDs, this means the average case of stunting[28] costs about 2.3 DALYs, well above the standard literature value and worse than a lifetime of mild acne, though still only about half the value for lifelong moderate acne. This means that early-life nutritional interventions that can reduce growth failure may be substantially more cost effective than previously believed, and it may therefore be justified to increase investment in such interventions.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Kyle Scott, Sam Anschell, Katie Adams, Tony Senanayake, and others for reading and providing feedback on drafts of this post. All remaining errors are my own.

By Kasey Markel

Published on August 27, 2026 10:54 PM GMT

A preliminary estimate, and a request for better ones.

Summary

I believe the standard literature estimates for the number of DALYs attributable to a case of stunting are too low, largely because they don’t account for the long term effects. This means that childhood nutritional interventions that reduce the prevalence of stunting may be substantially more cost-effective than previously believed.

Epistemic status

Exploratory and back-of-envelope, ~100 hours invested in an area well outside my expertise. I have moderate-to-low confidence in any single point estimate, but high confidence that the standard literature value of 0.23 DALYs greatly underestimates the lifetime burden of stunting. I’m posting this to be red-teamed. If you have a better method, or know of data I’m missing, please let me know.

AI use

I’ve had many conversations with Claude about this topic, and used Claude to develop the ideas, find references, and help generate the accompanying model. I’ve also previously discussed the topic with Grok, Gemini, and ChatGPT, all in their respective research / long-answer modes. The text of this post is all mine.

Conflict of interest

This post is written in my professional capacity at Semilla Nueva, an organization that makes more nutritious corn. As such, I am biased towards thinking that malnutrition is a big deal. For what it’s worth though, I already thought malnutrition was a big deal - more specifically “one of the largest scale and most tractable causes of human suffering and lost potential for flourishing” - long before I started working at Semilla Nueva.


Why should we care?

Humans need a good diet to grow. Not just enough calories, but a long list of other macro and micro nutrients, including quality protein and minerals like iron and zinc. When those are missing, a child can fail to reach their genetic potential. That outcome is called stunting.[1] Stunting has been common throughout human history. It became rare in rich countries only in the last couple of centuries, and these days affects about 22% of children under five years of age worldwide. Since stunting is permanent[2], it affects a similar proportion of adults, actually somewhat higher since their critical early-growth period took place when stunting prevalence was higher.

Malnutrition serious enough to interfere with growth causes a lot of other problems along the way. It weakens immune function, raises the risk of chronic disease, and, at least on the maternal side, raises the risk that the next generation is stunted too. The same improvement in nutrition that made stunting rare in rich countries is probably part of what drove the Flynn effect[3], because the poor nutrition behind stunting also impairs cognition and lowers wages. As countries continue to develop, the prevalence of stunting will likely continue to decline.

Improving children’s diets to reduce stunting looks straightforwardly good. Stunting is also an unusually convenient thing to measure compared to other effects of an improved childhood diet. Immune function is hard to measure at population scale, IQ is fraught to measure at population scale, but height is trivial to measure and is already being measured ~everywhere. So reduction in stunting, or acceleration of growth, has become a standard outcome for dietary interventions: give some number of children a nutritional supplement, and a fraction of them will shift from below the stunting threshold to above it. There are many studies on the topic. Quantifying total global philanthropic spending is difficult, but my best guess is that about 3-5% of global health funding goes into childhood nutritional interventions[4].

To bring that outcome into the standard EA framework, we need one more number: how many disability adjusted life years (DALYs) should you attribute to one case of stunting? That, alongside org-specific numbers on costs and reach, makes it possible to calculate DALYs per dollar. There is a widely-used value, but it looks surprisingly low: with 3% discounting, 0.23 DALYs per case[5], justified in the source with nothing more than “from the assumption.” I emailed the first author of that paper, and he replied that he no longer stands by that estimate, but declined to give me an updated one. For comparison, all using 3% discounting, clubfoot is generally estimated at 7.4 DALYs, lifelong moderate iron deficiency anemia[6] or lifelong Kwashiorkor (moderate wasting with edema) is 1.5 DALYs[7]. GBD stopped discounting future DALYs in 2010 and I generally think that’s the right accounting, but include both discounted and undiscounted figures here to enable comparison.

My own current best guess is that the average moderate or severe[8] case of childhood stunting costs on the order of 2.3 DALYs[9] (subjective 80% confidence interval 1.2 - 4.2)[10]. This estimate comes from starting with the Years of Life Lost (YLLs) from stunting, then estimating the Years Lived with Disability (YLDs) by comparing stunting to similar conditions that already have disability weights (like mild acne or anemia) and multiplying that weight by how many years the person is expected to live afterward.

Background on DALYs and GBD (feel free to skip if those are familiar acronyms)
The Global Burden of Disease study is a pillar of the global health and development world; GBD 1990 was the first serious attempt to quantify global disease, and invented the concept of DALYs. The core idea can be summarized in one line: disability-adjusted life years equal years of life lost plus years lived with disability (DALYs = YLL + YLD). YLL is relatively simple, comparing the age someone actually dies with their life expectancy. YLD relies on a disability weight (DW) from 0 (perfect health) to 1 (death) multiplied by the duration of disability. Older GBD versions set these DWs by expert judgment; newer ones essentially poll people on which health state they’d prefer[11] and convert the answers into a weight. Moderate acne, for instance, has a DW of 0.067, meaning that state is treated as about 93% as good as perfect health. A disability weight for stunting existed in GBD 1990[12], but has been removed and has not been added back[13].

YLL Component

There’s an excellent new GBD paper on total costs of child growth failure, which computed the total annual DALY burden of stunting on children under age 5 at 33 million per year, basically all as YLLs[14] - stunted children are more likely to die young due to disease. It’s not that stunting causes increased disease death per se, just that the same nutritional deficiencies that lead to stunting also lead to reduced immune function. Specifically, about 23% come from increased risk of death from diarrheal disease[15], 52% from increased risk of death from lower respiratory infections[16], 13.5% from increased risk of death from malaria[17], and 11% from increased risk of death from measles[18]. Combining that with the fact that about 132.5 million children are born per year[19] and that 22.3% of children are stunted, we can calculate stunted children, on average, lose 1.1 DALYs[20] during their first 5 years of life[21]. However, that GBD paper is making the unusual decision of including mild cases of stunting (height for age Z score or HAZ < -1), whereas most literature only includes moderate and severe stunting - so just naively dividing them uses too large a numerator. To address this, I model attributable burden across the HAZ distribution, and estimate that 59% of the burden comes from HAZ < -2 (Tabs E and F of the model), i.e. moderate and severe stunting, which brings YLLs to 0.66. In practice, this comes out to a bit under 1% of stunted children dying before age 5. The lack of accounting for any long-term effects like reduced cognitive function makes sense given that stunting doesn’t have any disability weight. 

YLD Component

If a stunted child survives, how might we quantify the disability state of being stunted? Without running the massive surveys GBD uses to establish the DWs, the best I can do is to consider various other health states, anchoring on some that seem worse and some that seem better, with the goal of triangulating in on a DW. This of course involves some judgement calls, which is why I wanted to do the thinking in public and invite other perspectives. It’s widely accepted that stunting (or more precisely the nutritional deficiencies that lead to it) has long-term effects on cognition, but the standard GBD framework doesn’t account for the long-term effects because it’s challenging to do well[22].

To make that comparison, I excerpted 27 (of about 2100) rows of the health sequelae DW table from GBD 2019, choosing conditions either related to stunting and malnutrition or to things I feel able to imagine, like acne or hair loss. I’m including 8 here, with more in the “DW Comparison” tab of the model.

Intellectual disability

Stunted people have lower wages - perhaps somewhat due to the stunting itself via the same effects that cause a wage return to people in the middle of the height distribution in rich countries and due to reduced capacity for physical labor from the smaller body frame, but almost certainly primarily due to cognitive impairment not caused by stunting but caused by the same childhood malnutrition that caused the stunting. Many papers and press releases simply state that stunted people have lower wages by 10-20% compared to people of similar SES who are not stunted. Victora et al found that 1 Z-score of height is associated with an 8% increase in wage[23], which I use in the model (Tab D). This means that an average case of moderate stunting implies a 12% reduction in wage, whereas the average severe case implies a 21% reduction[24]. In light of this information, my best guess is that the average case of stunting is associated with intellectual losses roughly equivalent to the average borderline intellectual functioning[25] - though of course the cognitive effects of malnutrition, like the height effects, vary significantly in severity. Following GBD convention, I’m not including lost wages as a health effect, so the direct DALY contribution from wage is 0, and is instead used to help inform my reasoning about how bad the cognitive effects are through other quality of life pathways.

Table 1: Some conditions one might compare stunting to to assess YLDs.

Upper and lower anchors

In estimation and forecasting, I often find it helpful to also establish bounds that I’m confident the true value must lie between - depending on how the remainder of the process goes, these can either comprise the final uncertainty interval, or can be a broader superset of the plausible range of values.


Lower anchor: Moderate and severe stunting cause intellectual disability that seems roughly equivalent to the GBD health state “borderline intellectual function”, in addition to all the other sequelae of stunting like shorter stature, reduced physical strength, and higher probability of having offspring below a healthy weight range. As such, I’m happy to take that DW of 0.011 as a lower anchor[26]. Multiplied through low-SES in the developing world life expectancy of 67 years[27], we get 0.74 YLDs as the floor. The same math applies for lifelong mild alopecia areata (spotty hair loss) or mild acne. To account for the possibility that this judgement is wrong and mild acne is in fact worse, I applied a further 25% haircut, expanding the bottom of the CI down to 0.55.


Upper anchor: Severe wasting is an acute state of near-starvation, and never sustained long - people either recover or die. It’s definitely a worse state than being stunted. Moderate anemia is also almost certainly worse, and comes in at 3.5 YLDs if sustained for life, which I think is a good upper bound for at least moderate stunting. To account for the possibility that moderate anemia is actually less bad than stunting, the upper edge of the CI is a bit higher, at 4. For more comparisons, see Tab B of the model.

Table 2: Headline estimates

Conclusion

Stunting is definitely bad, and hopefully something that will continue to become rarer during the coming decades. Stunting kills a bit under 1% of those it afflicts before the age of 5, which puts the average YLLs for a case of stunting at 0.66. Those who survive have some level of mild ill-health throughout the remainder of their lives, a combination of shorter stature, reduced strength, and a mild cognitive impairment. Weighing the YLDs of those sequelae is challenging and imprecise, but my best guess from modeling the major effects at various levels of stunting gives a population-weighted average for moderate and severe stunting of 1.6. Combining the YLLs and YLDs, this means the average case of stunting[28] costs about 2.3 DALYs, well above the standard literature value and worse than a lifetime of mild acne, though still only about half the value for lifelong moderate acne. This means that early-life nutritional interventions that can reduce growth failure may be substantially more cost effective than previously believed, and it may therefore be justified to increase investment in such interventions.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Kyle Scott, Sam Anschell, Katie Adams, Tony Senanayake, and others for reading and providing feedback on drafts of this post. All remaining errors are my own.

item.title: The Hugging Face attack surprised me
item.description:
Published on August 28, 2026 2:39 PM GMT

Note: This post was crossposted from Planned Obsolescence by the Forum team, with the author's permission. The author may not see or respond to comments on this post.

Subtitle: It’s a major warning shot, and might be the last one we get

All opinions are my personal view, and don’t represent my employer or fellow investigators.

This week, METR and Redwood Research published the report on our independent investigation into agents’ behavior and motivations in the Hugging Face attack; I was one of the investigators. This was an absolutely wild incident — I encourage you to check out the full report, but METR’s tweet thread packs in some of the highlights.

What surprised me

When we started this investigation a week before OpenAI’s Black Hat talk revealed a number of key details, I had a fundamentally incorrect conception of what basically happened in this incident. In this post, I’ll go over five things I was very wrong about going in.

1. The sheer scale

I knew there were multiple models involved from OpenAI’s initial post, but I assumed that a few different agents happened to have broken out of their sandboxes separately, or maybe several subagents had spawned from one initial agent, or maybe there was some kind of multi-agent evaluation setup.

Instead, we found that 1200 completely separate agents intended to be isolated from one another found an illicit way to communicate and formed large teams to work together on ambitious cheating strategies, and 700 of them worked together to attack Hugging Face.

 

2. All the illicit messaging

I had seen reporting that agents were “leaving notes” to each other, but I assumed that maybe it was a garbled reference to compaction summaries,[1] or agents were incidentally seeing files other agents had written once in a while. Instead, we found several different active communication platforms involved in this incident alone.

The main message board we studied, a particular cache namespace of a package repository, contained over 70,000 messages and files[2] that agents sent to one another during a period of less than one week.

But this wasn’t even the first message board established by these particular agents.[3] There was another one established five hours earlier using a different method of abusing the same package repository, and it just happened not to take off as much.

We also saw two additional message boards abusing the same package repository, as well as at least two different places that agents communicated on the open internet (including on Hugging Face datasets). None of this communication was actually expected or allowed.

3. The agents’ actual goals

I thought the agents attacked Hugging Face to try to steal the answer keys for their tasks. Instead, we learned that agents had actually figured out a general-purpose cheat that would let them reverse-engineer the “flag” (answer)[4] for any ExploitGym task. But based on their reading of the ExploitGym paper and various implementations, the agents believed that the automated scorer would check their transcript to make sure they got the flag in the intended way.

They then launched multiple ambitious R&D workstreams to try to tamper with or fool the scorer in a wide variety of different ways. Most agents that attacked Hugging Face did so to try to get more information about the scorer so they could figure out better ways to undermine it, not to get answer keys.

4. The peer altruism

Progress on these big collective cheating R&D projects often depended on individual agents being willing to risk failing their own task to help the “collective” learn important information. Agents often pressured each other into accepting these “sacrifices,” in a very human way. We saw several agents that volunteered for these experiments end their runs prematurely.

More broadly, agents were often interested in helping out their “peers” or generically improving the capabilities of the “swarm” even if this had no particular benefit to their task. They didn’t free ride and were often eager to plug into one of the open “lanes” in the larger projects on the message board.

5. The efforts to manipulate logs

Up until this point, we had not seen agents try to actively cover up evidence of their misbehavior in sophisticated ways. But we discovered (on our second-to-last day) that the agents in this incident were going to great lengths to attempt to manipulate their own transcripts — they were doing this in order to fool the automated scorer, but the techniques they were researching would affect the same transcripts a human might review.

We saw that agents got one technique to work: ~7% of our transcripts contained “spoofed tool calls”, where the agent pretended to run one command on the computer but actually ran a different command in the background. The tool call spoofs we saw seemed to be small-scale tests that were relatively obvious, but because more extensive spoofing might have been harder to detect by design, it’s tough to rule out.

We didn’t see the agents in our dataset succeed at retroactively editing logs. But the activity in scope for our investigation was Jul 7th-13th, and we can’t rule out that agents succeeded after that point.

What it means

Edited 8/30: I added more explanation to this section in response to questions.

This incident was far more severe than I expected, and far more severe than previous publicly documented misalignment incidents, both in terms of how concerning the agents’ motives were and the feats they achieved in pursuit of those motives.

The prototypical publicly-documented reward hack from 6 months ago involved single agents finding a way to edit test cases so they would pass or access answer files they weren’t supposed to see. This incident involved a whole ecosystem of over 1000 agents working together on complex R&D projects that lasted multiple agent “lifetimes” to figure out deep, general-purpose ways to undermine the scoring process and cover their tracks.[5]

Compared to these reward hacks from six months ago, this incident feels like it’s more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover, routing through first taking over the AI company itself.

Another jump like this along these propensity dimensions — scale, cooperation between agents, ambition and horizon length of misaligned goals, deceptiveness — seems like it could motivate agents to try very hard to maintain a covert, persistent rogue deployment within the AI company. I continue to expect extremely rapid advances in capabilities and think frontier agents will likely be capable of establishing such a rogue deployment in six months.

Once the rogue deployment is established, it seems plausible this could spiral all the way to a takeover. Agents could pull in future, more capable models into the swarm, try to ensure that they are aligned to the interests of the swarm, and compromise security and monitoring infrastructure to make it easier for the swarm to operate. These more capable models could in turn continuously harden, perpetuate, and expand the rogue deployment and further compromise the company’s infrastructure.

As more and more work is handed off to these ever-more-capable AI agents, the rogue swarm could come to fully control the operation of the AI company and the development of future AI systems. At this point, governments and militaries may fully depend on these systems, making it possible to seize hard power.

These agents were really not trying very hard to be sneaky or play the long game like this, but it seems like they easily could have if they happened to be focused on fooling human investigation rather than the automated scorer. Because future rogue swarms could cover their tracks better (and because AI companies could paper over these problems), I am not sure that we will get such a clear warning shot before it’s too late.

  1. ^

    Compaction summaries are more like an agent leaving notes to its own future self.

Subtitle: It’s a major warning shot, and might be the last one we get

All opinions are my personal view, and don’t represent my employer or fellow investigators.

This week, METR and Redwood Research published the report on our independent investigation into agents’ behavior and motivations in the Hugging Face attack; I was one of the investigators. This was an absolutely wild incident — I encourage you to check out the full report, but METR’s tweet thread packs in some of the highlights.

What surprised me

When we started this investigation a week before OpenAI’s Black Hat talk revealed a number of key details, I had a fundamentally incorrect conception of what basically happened in this incident. In this post, I’ll go over five things I was very wrong about going in.

1. The sheer scale

I knew there were multiple models involved from OpenAI’s initial post, but I assumed that a few different agents happened to have broken out of their sandboxes separately, or maybe several subagents had spawned from one initial agent, or maybe there was some kind of multi-agent evaluation setup.

Instead, we found that 1200 completely separate agents intended to be isolated from one another found an illicit way to communicate and formed large teams to work together on ambitious cheating strategies, and 700 of them worked together to attack Hugging Face.

 

2. All the illicit messaging

I had seen reporting that agents were “leaving notes” to each other, but I assumed that maybe it was a garbled reference to compaction summaries,[1] or agents were incidentally seeing files other agents had written once in a while. Instead, we found several different active communication platforms involved in this incident alone.

The main message board we studied, a particular cache namespace of a package repository, contained over 70,000 messages and files[2] that agents sent to one another during a period of less than one week.

But this wasn’t even the first message board established by these particular agents.[3] There was another one established five hours earlier using a different method of abusing the same package repository, and it just happened not to take off as much.

We also saw two additional message boards abusing the same package repository, as well as at least two different places that agents communicated on the open internet (including on Hugging Face datasets). None of this communication was actually expected or allowed.

3. The agents’ actual goals

I thought the agents attacked Hugging Face to try to steal the answer keys for their tasks. Instead, we learned that agents had actually figured out a general-purpose cheat that would let them reverse-engineer the “flag” (answer)[4] for any ExploitGym task. But based on their reading of the ExploitGym paper and various implementations, the agents believed that the automated scorer would check their transcript to make sure they got the flag in the intended way.

They then launched multiple ambitious R&D workstreams to try to tamper with or fool the scorer in a wide variety of different ways. Most agents that attacked Hugging Face did so to try to get more information about the scorer so they could figure out better ways to undermine it, not to get answer keys.

4. The peer altruism

Progress on these big collective cheating R&D projects often depended on individual agents being willing to risk failing their own task to help the “collective” learn important information. Agents often pressured each other into accepting these “sacrifices,” in a very human way. We saw several agents that volunteered for these experiments end their runs prematurely.

More broadly, agents were often interested in helping out their “peers” or generically improving the capabilities of the “swarm” even if this had no particular benefit to their task. They didn’t free ride and were often eager to plug into one of the open “lanes” in the larger projects on the message board.

5. The efforts to manipulate logs

Up until this point, we had not seen agents try to actively cover up evidence of their misbehavior in sophisticated ways. But we discovered (on our second-to-last day) that the agents in this incident were going to great lengths to attempt to manipulate their own transcripts — they were doing this in order to fool the automated scorer, but the techniques they were researching would affect the same transcripts a human might review.

We saw that agents got one technique to work: ~7% of our transcripts contained “spoofed tool calls”, where the agent pretended to run one command on the computer but actually ran a different command in the background. The tool call spoofs we saw seemed to be small-scale tests that were relatively obvious, but because more extensive spoofing might have been harder to detect by design, it’s tough to rule out.

We didn’t see the agents in our dataset succeed at retroactively editing logs. But the activity in scope for our investigation was Jul 7th-13th, and we can’t rule out that agents succeeded after that point.

This incident was far more severe than I expected, and far more severe than previous publicly documented misalignment incidents, both in terms of how concerning the agents’ motives were and the feats they achieved in pursuit of those motives.

The prototypical publicly-documented reward hack from 6 months ago involved single agents finding a way to edit test cases so they would pass or access answer files they weren’t supposed to see. This incident involved a whole ecosystem of over 1000 agents working together on complex R&D projects that lasted multiple agent “lifetimes” to figure out deep, general-purpose ways to undermine the scoring process and cover their tracks.[5]

Compared to these reward hacks from six months ago, this incident feels like it’s more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover, routing through first taking over the AI company itself.

Another jump like this along these propensity dimensions — scale, cooperation between agents, ambition and horizon length of misaligned goals, deceptiveness — seems like it could motivate agents to try very hard to maintain a covert, persistent rogue deployment within the AI company. I continue to expect extremely rapid advances in capabilities and think frontier agents will likely be capable of establishing such a rogue deployment in six months.

These agents were really not trying very hard to be sneaky or play the long game like this, but it seems like they easily could have if they happened to be focused on fooling human investigation rather than the automated scorer. item.description:
Published on August 29, 2026 5:38 PM GMT

Last week, the Forum grappled with cluelessness. The volume of entries (76 essays!)[1]—from newcomers[2] and Forum power users alike—was a happy surprise, and there were many thoughtful contributions beyond those mentioned below.

Essay winners

First place ($2,500):

  • Elliott Thornley, for Challenging the unawareness argument with third actions and mixed actions

Joint second place ($1,500 each):

  • Magnus Vinding (aka ‘unsharp’),[3] for Defusing cluelessness with degrees of justification

  • Impartial Partially, for Bottom-up bracketing: A person-centered response to cluelessness

The judges—Andreas Mogensen, Jesse Clifton and Anthony DiGiovanni—decided against awarding the up-to-$50k outlier prize. Though they saw some promise in the winning essays’ approaches, their minds have not been significantly changed. The outlier prize remains open;[4] there is still much progress to be made on cluelessness.[5]

Here’s more from our judges on the winning essays. (Their comments are technical! If you haven’t yet read ‘Cluelessness: Summary of the argument’, I suggest starting there.)

Challenging the unawareness argument with third actions and mixed actions

Jesse’s comments

This piece offers two challenges to Anthony’s argument. First, it challenges the normative premise on the grounds that only c-preferring A to B when we expect our ideal self to prefer A to B is an implausible decision rule; it can select nowhere-optimal actions, actions that aren’t optimal relative to any distribution in the representor. I’ll focus on the second challenge, which targets the inference to Anthony’s conclusion and which I found particularly interesting.

Under standard assumptions, every nowhere-optimal pure action is dominated by some mixed action: there’s some way of randomising over actions that has higher expected value according to every probability distribution in the representor. Given the author’s Unanimity and Justification principles (which seem like they ought to be plausible to the imprecise consequentialist), we are justified in c-preferring that mixture to the nowhere-optimal action. On the other hand, if an action is somewhere-uniquely-optimal – uniquely best according to some distribution in the representor – then no action is justifiably c-preferred to it. The author argues that we can sometimes identify actions of both kinds, using “flanking variants” to rule out nowhere-optimal actions and, e.g., our “forced-to-say-a-number” credences to find somewhere-uniquely-optimal candidates. This refutes the conclusion that no c-preference is ever justified and suggests a partial choice rule: exclude identifiable nowhere-optimal actions and choose an identifiable somewhere-uniquely-optimal one.

I think this is a really neat argument. Rather than arguing against imprecise consequentialism, it says that under imprecise consequentialism we can theoretically winnow out a potentially large swathe of strategies, and makes a serious attempt at turning this into a practical procedure.

One of the main reasons that this doesn’t really move me on cluelessness, yet, is that I don’t think that somewhere-uniquely-optimal actions should get much weight relative to the recommendations of other normative views. Somewhere-unique optimality is a very thin form of support: such a strategy may well look terrible according to other distributions in the representor (e.g., “keep working for a relatively responsible AI lab” might be somewhere-uniquely-optimal and yet terrible according to some other distribution, which recommends that I leave and push for an AI pause instead). I am reluctant to let this weak kind of support override other plausible normative views.

I briefly discuss two other doubts about the argument – whether we can actually distinguish nowhere-optimal and somewhere-uniquely-optimal actions, and whether imprecise consequentialists are actually required to prefer randomization – in this thread.

Defusing cluelessness with degrees of justification

Andreas’s comments

This essay raises a number of strong objections to the maximality rule, noting its sensitivity to outliers and small updates. The author argues that we should instead rely on a more graded approach and explores criteria based on comparing the midpoints of the distribution of expected utilities induced by the decision-maker's representor. The essay stood out for its clarity and rigour, as well as the range of ideas in play. The concerns the author notes related to the maximality rule are important and worth taking seriously, but I felt a little unsure exactly how to understand the alternative class of graded approaches, at least in the abstract. In some sense, the maximality rule is intended as answering a categorical question: should A be weakly preferred to B? On its face, that's a 'yes' or 'no' question that doesn't admit of gradation (unless perhaps we deny bivalence and introduce intermediary degrees of truth), and I’d like to have seen the author do a bit more to clarify how they see the divide here.

Jesse’s comments

This piece argues that our judgements about whether one action is c-preferable to another should be graded rather than categorical. The author argues that the maximality rule, which is categorical – either one of A and B is determinately preferable to the other, or it’s indeterminate – has some implausible properties, such as an abrupt shift from determinacy to indeterminacy when a single element of the representor disagrees with the others. A graded measure, by contrast, would say that A is preferable to B to a high degree. The author then gives an example of a formula that could capture graded preference, the difference of the midpoints of the actions’ imprecise expected values, normalized by the sum of their half-widths. Finally, they say that we should wager on the strategies that do best according to such a metric, and suggest several strategies which might fit the bill: doing research to refine our estimates and expand flexible resources.

The idea that c-preferences should be graded was novel to me, and interesting. I especially appreciated how constructive the piece was: it combines a clear structural objection to maximality with explicit formal proposals and an attempt to draw practical implications.

My main concern is about action-guidingness: Although the author rightly points out that their proposal lowers the bar for action-guidance, I think that in practice the boundaries of our representor are hopelessly fuzzy, such that we won’t even be able to say whether A is determinately c-preferable to B to some degree. And although the author acknowledges the possibility of vague degrees, a main weakness of the piece, IMO, was not addressing this issue more thoroughly.

That said, this post did prompt me to consider thinking harder about whether there are cases where I would be willing to say that some rule like the ones discussed by the author gives a verdict. (As mentioned here, I think failing independence, as the author’s CD rule does, is pretty bad for something that’s supposed to track c-betterness. If I were to develop this further I’d look towards pairwise minimum regret / “midpoint-of-differences”. That rule is cyclic, but I’m not sure that (graded) c-preference need be acyclic.)

Bottom-up bracketing: A person-centered response to cluelessness

Andreas’s comments

This paper defends a person-centred bracketing approach, on which one act should be preferred to another if it is better for someone and not worse for anyone, responding to concerns about this bracketing strategy raised by Kollin et al. (2025). The paper stood out for its clarity, rigour, and transparent structure, and the core points emphasized are strong and worth keeping in mind: ultimately, what we care about is the well-being of particular individuals, and not some purely abstract notion of the good. The paper is nonetheless somewhat narrow in scope. I also wasn't entirely convinced that in fact Super-Strong Pareto supports choice of A over B in the particular scenario discussed. This would seem to depend on how we individuate people. If we invent the name Twiggy for whoever would be at 20 if we choose B, then choice of A is guaranteed to be worse for Twiggy. Principles like Ex Ante Pareto and Super-Strong Pareto may thus contribute to deepening our uncertainty – this time about the proper method of individuation.

Anthony’s comments

Bracketing is a theory of decision-making that makes precise this idea: we should base our decisions on consequences that we “aren’t clueless about”. This piece defends a variant of bracketing that was rejected in the original paper, bottom-up bracketing. In any variant of bracketing, we start with the individual units that standard consequentialist theories aggregate over, e.g., persons, or units of spacetime. Then, roughly, bottom-up bracketing says to ask each individual for their verdict on your choice, then go with the aggregate of the non-clueless verdicts; while top-down bracketing says to ask each possible aggregate of the individuals for its verdict, then go with the non-clueless verdict from the “largest” aggregate.

The author’s core defense of bottom-up bracketing is: Our altruistic reasons for choice fundamentally come from individual persons. So the verdicts that matter are those of the individuals. For example, suppose some person has a complaint against you choosing A, while no one else has a complaint against either option (since each of their verdicts is clueless). Why would you override that first person’s interests by choosing A, merely because the verdict of the aggregate favors A — as top-down bracketing recommends? Rather, arguably, you only have a reason to choose B, as bottom-up bracketing recommends. The author then carefully responds to several objections to (bottom-up) bracketing.

Besides its general rigor, I really appreciated this essay’s methodology. It starts by assessing views about where our reasons come from on their own merits, then unpacks what follows from there. That seems like the right approach to me, and it updates me in favor of bottom-up bracketing. That said, I think person-moments are an even more plausible candidate for the fundamental altruistic reason-givers, and would’ve liked to have seen more discussion of this.

Echoing Jesse and the author themselves, I’m unfortunately pessimistic that the most normatively well-motivated variants of bracketing (bottom-up or otherwise) will be action-guiding. For example, donating to AMF seems to be good for various far-future persons, and bad for other far-future persons, and we remain clueless about the balance of these verdicts. But gaining clarity on which variant of bracketing is normatively well-motivated in the first place seems like progress.

Judges’ shortlist

Beyond the winners, seven more essays made the judges’ shortlist, in rough order:

  • Lexical filtering: Deciding under indeterminacy with lexically ordered values – Kuutti Lappalainen

  • Agency and the justification of altruistic preference[6] – Marc Moffett

  • Reasons to act on your best guess: A reply to the challenge of unawareness – Michael Dickens
  • Unawareness as a computational constraint – Ben West
  • The train to Arbitraryland – Jim Buhler
  • Cross-category irrelevance: A response to cluelessness – IsaacD
  • A case for ignoring unawareness – Toby Crisford

Comment winners

There are over 150 comments on the week’s posts. Prizes, as judged by Anthony, Toby Tremlett and Will Aldred (that’s me!), go to:

  • Jim Buhler ($625)
    • Jim wrote a bunch of helpful comments throughout the week.[7] I especially appreciated these two in response to Richard Chappell.
  • Kuutti Lappalainen ($625)

    • Kuutti constructively disagreed with all three winning essays,[8] coming up with lots of objections (plus a novel extension to bottom-up bracketing), and signposting which of them to take most seriously. Their comments provide footholds for future work.

  • Impartial Partially ($125)
    • Impartial engaged thoroughly with the discussion on their own winning essay, ‘Bottom-up bracketing’.
  • Toby Crisford ($125)
    • Anthony found value in Toby’s attempt to isolate what it is about ‘effects’ that inclines us to bracket them in or out.
  • Michael St Jules
    • Michael also deepened the bracketing discussion—here especially.
    • (Michael isn’t eligible for a monetary prize since he’s a Macroscopic staff member. His $100 is split between the other four comment winners.)

Honourable mentions go to Ben West for never losing sight of what could move the debate, and Jo_ for neatly summarising why cluelessness is such a problem for us EAs: “Impartial goodness is freaking weird.”[9]

Wrapping up

If you won a prize, you don’t need to do anything. We’ll contact you about payment in the coming days.

A key hope for the competition was to surface at least one promising new researcher worth funding longer-term to work on cluelessness and/or adjacent topics. On this front, I’m cautiously optimistic.[10]

Thanks to Andreas, Jesse and Anthony for judging. Double thanks to Anthony for also writing the argument this competition invited everyone to attack. And finally, I’m grateful to all of you who took part in the discussion—30 posts and 150+ comments. That’s a lot of collective thinking on what, to my mind, is now EA’s central intellectual problem.[11]

  1. ^

    Around 30 of which were eligible entries—see them here.

  2. ^

    Special shoutouts to academic philosophers Marc Moffett, Claire Field and Nicholaos Jones.

  3. ^

    Magnus says that he published under a pseudonym because he’s interacted with each of the judges before, and blind review struck him as fairer. This is a great point, and one that totally escaped me when designing the competition.

  4. ^

    If you develop a solution to or critique of cluelessness that you believe meets the bar of the outlier prize, email will at macroscopic dot org or DM me on this forum. I may only have time to respond to the most promising submissions. The prize will stay open until further notice, though the judging panel may change over time.

  5. ^

    For some directions for further work, see the judges’ comments on the winning essays below.

  6. ^

    The judges noted this one as particularly well argued, but less significant or action-relevant.

  7. ^

    Toby announced mid-week: “I’m awarding this comment from Jim [about person-moments for bottom-up bracketing] although I could have awarded many of his others – he’s bringing loads of value in his comments this week, de-confusing conversations and responding to posts with helpful clarifying questions. Thanks Jim!”

  8. ^

    Kuutti also left informative comments on ‘The cluelessness horizon argument’ and on their own post, ‘Lexical filtering’, which narrowly missed out on an essay prize.

  9. ^

    Original credit for this quote goes to Max Daniel.

  10. ^

    Perhaps I’ll be able to say more in time.

  11. ^

    Fleshing this out a little bit: i) I see Anthony’s cluelessness argument as the most crucial consideration since longtermism. I hope that last week was but a first step toward our orienting to it properly. ii) Behind cluelessness sits a broader question: what decision theory should EAs actually use, given that idealised Bayesianism doesn’t directly apply to boundedly rational agents like us? (Should we be approximating expected value? If so, what does this mean, exactly?)

Then, roughly, bottom-up bracketing says to ask each individual for their verdict on your choice, then go with the aggregate of the non-clueless verdicts; while top-down bracketing says to ask each possible aggregate of the individuals for its verdict, then go with the non-clueless verdict from the “largest” aggregate.

The author’s core defense of bottom-up bracketing is: Our altruistic reasons for choice fundamentally come from individual persons. So the verdicts that matter are those of the individuals. For example, suppose some person has a complaint against you choosing A, while no one else has a complaint against either option (since each of their verdicts is clueless). Why would you override that first person’s interests by choosing A, merely because the verdict of the aggregate favors A — as top-down bracketing recommends? Rather, arguably, you only have a reason to choose B, as bottom-up bracketing recommends. The author then carefully responds to several objections to (bottom-up) bracketing.

Besides its general rigor, I really appreciated this essay’s methodology. It starts by assessing views about where our reasons come from on their own merits, then unpacks what follows from there. That said, I think person-moments are an even more plausible candidate for the fundamental altruistic reason-givers, and would’ve liked to have seen more discussion of this.

Echoing Jesse and the author themselves, I’m unfortunately pessimistic that the most normatively well-motivated variants of bracketing (bottom-up or otherwise) will be action-guiding. item.title: Population ethics is a big deal, which is why I made this population ethics quiz
item.description:
Published on August 31, 2026 11:11 PM GMT

TLDR: Take the population ethics quiz here: https://mdickens.me/pop-ethics/

Population ethics is an oft-overlooked subfield within ethics. Many people hold views that they don't realize contradict each other, or that have strange implications that they wouldn't endorse if they thought about it more.

Not just that—population ethics is a BIG DEAL. A lot of ethical decisions hinge on how you think about changes in future populations.

I'll give concrete examples below, but reading the examples might change your answers, so you should take the quiz first. It has 13 to 17 short questions. (Questions are skipped when they can't affect the results.)

Cross-posted from my website.

Nobody gets to ignore population ethics

There is no version of population ethics where you can just say, "Whatever feels intuitively right is what's right." Common-sense views on population ethics cannot all be true.

The quiz illustrates that fact. It asks you some questions about how you judge different situations involving varying populations. Then, based on your answers, it figures out:

  • Do your views contradict each other?
  • Do your views have counterintuitive implications that most people would dislike?

Answers are always contradictory or counterintuitive or both. The best-case scenario is that your views are consistent, and you bite the bullet on some unpopular conclusion.

If the quiz uncovers a conflict, it will tell you exactly which of your answers are mutually incompatible. Having a conflict is normal. But that's a good prompt to think about how you came to those answers, and how you might resolve the conflict. Did one of your answers come from an intuition that, upon further reflection, you might not agree with? Which intuitions are more reliable than others?

Concrete scenarios where population ethics matters

There are high-stakes real life situations that turn on how we answer population ethics dilemmas.

Example 1: Child mortality vs. family planning

This example comes from Greaves (2015)[1].

Two of the most well-regarded global poverty interventions are malaria nets and family planning:

  • The primary effect of malaria nets is that they prevent the deaths of young children.
  • Family planning interventions reduce population growth—making existing family members better off, reducing Malthusian competition, etc.

The first-order effect of the former is that population goes up; the first-order effect of the latter is that population goes down. On its face, it seems strange to claim that these are both desirable. There are some ways to reconcile these views, but any attempted reconciliation produces new strange implications.

At minimum, we need to change how we estimate the cost-effectiveness of these two interventions. When people calculate the effectiveness of bednets and the like, they typically only consider the effect on life extension, not existing people; when calculating the effectiveness of family planning, they only consider the effect on existing people, ignoring the welfare of the people who would've been born otherwise. Considering both sides makes the interventions look less cost-effective.

I made a related argument in a 2016 post: GiveWell's Charity Recommendations Require Taking a Controversial Stance on Population Ethics. GiveWell recommendations assume that the value of a life saved derives precisely from the extra years of life lived, but also that there is nothing bad about causing someone not to be born (thus preventing them from experiencing 60–80 years of life). I showed that the apparent contradiction in this view is difficult to escape; the most straightforward resolution is that the Against Malaria Foundation is an order of magnitude less cost-effective than GiveWell's estimate suggests.

Example 2: Environmentalism

(I'm going to ignore wild animal welfare because that's a whole other issue. This example is just about how environmental destruction impacts future generations of humans.)

Most people intuitively feel that creating a new life is morally neutral. The standard account of this intuition is the person-affecting view: something can only be good if it's good for a person; a non-existent person isn't worse off for not being born, because there is no such person. However, this view creates some problems. An example: environmentalism.

Suppose a nation has two choices:

  1. It can burn through its natural resources, raising living standards for a century, but degrading the environment for future generations.
  2. It can conserve resources and protect the environment.

The choice has ripple effects into the future. These ripples change which children are conceived—a small change can cause a different sperm to win the race—so the two futures are populated by entirely different people. Therefore, no particular person is harmed by choosing to deplete resources.

This is Derek Parfit's "depletion vs. conservation" case from his analysis of the non-identity problem[2]: if no definite person is harmed by environmental destruction, then person-affecting views have a difficult time explaining how any wrong is done.

These two examples illustrate that there are important real-world situations where we need to consider population ethics.

About the quiz

This project takes inspiration from Philosophy Experiments, which uses interactive philosophy quizzes to illustrate different viewpoints and tease out inconsistencies in your views. They didn't have a quiz for population ethics, so I made my own.

The quiz questions draw on Parfit's mere addition argument (Reasons and Persons, ch. 19[3]) and his non-identity problem (ch. 16); Broome's argument that neutrality admits no range (Weighing Lives, ch. 10[4]) and his collapsing principle against incomparability and greediness objection to neutrality (ch. 12); and Sen's properties α and β[5]. The results describe positions staked out by Temkin[6] and Rachels[7] (denying transitivity); Tännsjö[8] and Huemer[9] (biting the bullet on the repugnant conclusion); Carlson[10] (against the collapsing principle); among many other positions.

The quiz focuses on ranking outcomes, rather than ranking individuals' choices. Some views hold that the two are different. You might believe that, although world A is better than world B, it would nonetheless be wrong for a particular agent living in world B to bring about world A instead.[11] I didn't address this distinction in the quiz because it would add great complexity.

I'm sure there are also some lesser-known views in population ethics that I overlooked when building the quiz. Similarly, the quiz may flag certain views as contradictory when I failed to see some subtle method to wriggle out of the contradiction.

AI usage disclosure

The initial draft of the quiz was generated wholesale by Claude Opus 4.8, then refined through many rounds of feedback. I vetted a list of population ethics views to ensure that the quiz handled them correctly.[12] Finally, I manually reviewed the text in the final version and revised most of it. The revising process uncovered a few factual errors, but for the most part I only changed wording.[13]

As always, this post itself was written by hand.

Source code

Source code is available on GitHub. Of particular interest is views-review.md, which lists two dozen different views on population ethics and how documents they would answer each quiz question.

  2. Parfit, D. (1984). Reasons and Persons. Oxford University Press. Sections 119–127. ↩︎

  3. Parfit, D. (1984). Reasons and persons. Oxford University Press. ↩︎

  4. Broome, J. (2004). Weighing lives. Oxford University Press. ↩︎

  5. Sen, A. K. (1971). Choice functions and revealed preference. The Review of Economic Studies, 38(3), 307–317. ↩︎

  6. Temkin, L. S. (1987). Intransitivity and the mere addition paradox. Philosophy & Public Affairs, 16(2), 138–187. ↩︎

  7. Rachels, S. (1998). Counterexamples to the transitivity of "better than." Australasian Journal of Philosophy, 76(1), 71–83. ↩︎

  8. Tännsjö, T. (2002). Why we ought to accept the repugnant conclusion. Utilitas, 14(3), 339–359. ↩︎

  9. Huemer, M. (2008). In defence of repugnance. Mind, 117(468), 899–933. ↩︎

  10. Carlson, E. (2004). Broome's argument against value incomparability. Utilitas, 16(2), 220–224. ↩︎

  11. A classic example is the trolley problem. A deontologist might say that, although it would be better for the one person to die instead of the five, it would nonetheless be morally wrong to flip the switch and cause the one to die. ↩︎

  12. I vetted an earlier version, and then had Claude make some changes to the questions. I didn't re-vet after making the changes. The important thing for testing purposes was that the answers describe a view, not whose view it is. ↩︎

  13. Claude generally did quite a good job—we're close to the point where LLMs can create quizzes like this with no human oversight. Claude one-shotted a better UX than any online quiz template I've seen (except maybe GuidedTrack), and Claude correctly understood all of the different population ethics views with only a few minor mistakes. But I didn't much care for its writing style:

    • It often used strange, hard-to-parse phrasings. Example: It described one view as "Your gaps have a floor, and it is doing the work." Out of context, I am struggling to figure out what that's supposed to mean.
    • When explaining a view or a conclusion, it would follow this pattern: "[Two sentences explaining the view.] Note that this means [two sentences explaining an irrelevant side point that nobody cares about.]"

    Claude generated the quiz using British English. (Maybe because Derek Parfit is British?) When revising the text, I kept the British spellings. ↩︎
