item.title: What happened to impact markets?
item.description:
Published on September 1, 2026 9:28 PM GMT

At a conference on post-AGI futures earlier this year, I proposed a session titled “What’s next for impact markets?” The conference speakers included the godfather of impact markets Paul Christiano himself, and noted supporters like Scott Alexander, Oli Habryka, and Andrew Critch — so I was hopeful that there would be some interest.

…

Zero people signed up for my session.

 

Before everyone writes these off as some EA fad of the early 2020s, or a pie-in-the-sky dream requiring impossible levels of funder buy-in: I’d like to give my account of what we’ve learned about impact markets, and where we can go next.

A brief oral history of Manifund

Our 501c3 entity “Manifold for Charity Inc.” was originally started with a narrow thesis: it’d be good to let Manifold prediction market traders donate winnings to a charity of their choice. See our original grant proposal to the FTX Future Fund, which they approved with a $500k grant around April 2022. But at the time, this was just a side project of Manifold.

Manifund proper was made with the explicit mandate of “make impact markets happen”. Scott Alexander was interested in trying out new mechanisms for funding projects, after the inaugural ACX Grants. I think he hated picking specific projects as winners himself, and wanted to absolve himself of this responsibility. (I’m pretty sympathetic to this btw.)

Scott and I were entranced by “impact markets” — Paul Christiano and Vitalik Buterin’s proposals for using retroactive funding and market-like equity mechanisms in nonprofit projects. Scott came up with the idea of an ACX “minigrants” round as an impact market, using forecasting as the specific subcategory that he and maybe Manifold had the ability to serve as retro funders for.

I convinced my then-girlfriend Rachel Weinberg to code up the v0 site with me, which we shipped in less than two weeks. (Trust me, this was impressive in the before-LLM-days.) Our idea was to operate like a scrappy tech startup; prove out the value of impact markets via small demonstrations; and have the best platform for hosting impact market rounds.

But after the initial launch and initial speculative funding round, we had nothing else to do for 6 months — while the grantees were working, before the all the projects were evaluated. It was then that Leopold Aschenbrenner, fresh off of FTX Future Fund, asked whether we would be interested in organizing FF-style regranting. He thought (and we agreed) that regranting was the best thing that Future Fund had invented. Mid 2023, he put us in touch with an aligned donor, and we were off to the races. With regranting, but also, with a more general-purpose “open call”, for any kind of grant application made in public — the Manifund that you see today.

In the years since, we’ve been busy with regranting, our general funding platform, and supporting a variety of grant programs — not to mention a festival series, community space, and software incubator. But impact markets remain part of Manifund’s founding motivation.

Wait, so, what do you think about impact markets now?

  1. Impact markets continue to be the best system we know of to coordinate philanthropy at scale. Markets can solve allocation problems that central planning can’t. In tech, markets have scaled to coordinate trillions of $ and tens of thousands of people; we want AI safety to do the same. As AI money floods philanthropy, now is the perfect time to revisit impact markets.
  2. However, Manifund’s original thesis of “small scale tests to prove out impact markets” didn’t pan out. At small scales, the whole endeavor isn’t really worth the complication. Angel-investor-like brainpower is scarce; coordination overhead is expensive. (I am optimistic that this could be somewhat mitigated today, since LLMs lowering the cost to price weird assets)
  3. A lot of the benefits of “impact markets” can be realized just by encouraging charitable founders to create C-Corps (or PBCs), which can take “investment” from nonprofit funders like AISTOF, or “revenue” from nonprofit buyers scoping out a prize or purchase commitment, like cG. We think this is better than defaulting to a nonprofit.

    C-Corps (and PBCs) offer case law and established norms for handling questions of compensation and allocation. Why futz around with impact markets if you can just start C-Corps?
  4. However, we’re currently in an ecosystem where much great AI safety work is done inside of 501c3 nonprofits like METR, Resolution, MATS, Lightcone. (And, ourselves, I hope.) So, to be backwards-compatible, we’re starting with concrete demonstrations of impact markets, to explain the concept to others and ourselves.

    If we can build trustworthy demonstrations via fake dollars, we expect to be able to convince donors that our calculations for “what is impactful” are better than anyone else’s. Call this the “early Givewell” approach towards impact markets: make lots of spreadsheets (ourselves, or with Claude); publish our work.
  5. Unlike early Givewell, the initial focus of our analysis might be intermediate funds rather than final charities. Which is to say, we might be better placed to say “should you donate to AISTOF vs Longview vs Lightcone Commons vs cG vs Macroscopic”, rather than “MATS vs Tarbell vs FAR”. (This rhymes with GWWC’s agenda of “evaluating the evaluators”, though we don’t think they’re doing much of this for AI safety). Our AI safety funder bulletin is an early example of this; Trace is another.
  6. Probably, the final retro buyer of impact will be God. And/or, the aligned future ASI.

In the short term, Manifund plans to continue improving philanthropy at the margins, eg by supporting regrantors and scaling up our core platform. But my ultimate goal for Manifund remains: to wholly align our society’s financial systems towards “doing good”. If you’d like to help, we’re hiring!

Our 501c3 entity “Manifold for Charity Inc.” was originally started with a narrow thesis: it’d be good to let Manifold prediction market traders donate winnings to a charity of their choice. See our original grant proposal to the FTX Future Fund, which they approved with a $500k grant around April 2022. But at the time, this was just a side project of Manifold.

Manifund proper was made with the explicit mandate of “make impact markets happen”. Scott Alexander was interested in trying out new mechanisms for funding projects, after the inaugural ACX Grants. I think he hated picking specific projects as winners himself, and wanted to absolve himself of this responsibility. (I’m pretty sympathetic to this btw.)

Scott and I were entranced by “impact markets” — Paul Christiano and Vitalik Buterin’s proposals for using retroactive funding and market-like equity mechanisms in nonprofit projects. Scott came up with the idea of an ACX “minigrants” round as an impact market, using forecasting as the specific subcategory that he and maybe Manifold had the ability to serve as retro funders for.

I convinced my then-girlfriend Rachel Weinberg to code up the v0 site with me, which we shipped in less than two weeks. (Trust me, this was impressive in the before-LLM-days.) Our idea was to operate like a scrappy tech startup; prove out the value of impact markets via small demonstrations; and have the best platform for hosting impact market rounds.

But after the initial launch and initial speculative funding round, we had nothing else to do for 6 months — while the grantees were working, before the all the projects were evaluated. It was then that Leopold Aschenbrenner, fresh off of FTX Future Fund, asked whether we would be interested in organizing FF-style regranting. He thought (and we agreed) that regranting was the best thing that Future Fund had invented. Mid 2023, he put us in touch with an aligned donor, and we were off to the races. With regranting, but also, with a more general-purpose “open call”, for any kind of grant application made in public — the Manifund that you see today.

In the years since, we’ve been busy with regranting, our general funding platform, and supporting a variety of grant programs — not to mention a festival series, community space, and software incubator. But impact markets remain part of Manifund’s founding motivation.

Wait, so, what do you think about impact markets now?

  1. Impact markets continue to be the best system we know of to coordinate philanthropy at scale. Markets can solve allocation problems that central planning can’t. In tech, markets have scaled to coordinate trillions of $ and tens of thousands of people; we want AI safety to do the same. As AI money floods philanthropy, now is the perfect time to revisit impact markets.
  2. However, Manifund’s original thesis of “small scale tests to prove out impact markets” didn’t pan out. At small scales, the whole endeavor isn’t really worth the complication. Angel-investor-like brainpower is scarce; coordination overhead is expensive. (I am optimistic that this could be somewhat mitigated today, since LLMs lowering the cost to price weird assets)
  3. A lot of the benefits of “impact markets” can be realized just by encouraging charitable founders to create C-Corps (or PBCs), which can take “investment” from nonprofit funders like AISTOF, or “revenue” from nonprofit buyers scoping out a prize or purchase commitment, like cG. We think this is better than defaulting to a nonprofit.

    C-Corps (and PBCs) offer case law and established norms for handling questions of compensation and allocation. Why futz around with impact markets if you can just start C-Corps?
  4. However, we’re currently in an ecosystem where much great AI safety work is done inside of 501c3 nonprofits like METR, Resolution, MATS, Lightcone. (And, ourselves, I hope.) So, to be backwards-compatible, we’re starting with concrete demonstrations of impact markets, to explain the concept to others and ourselves.

    If we can build trustworthy demonstrations via fake dollars, we expect to be able to convince donors that our calculations for “what is impactful” are better than anyone else’s. Call this the “early Givewell” approach towards impact markets: make lots of spreadsheets (ourselves, or with Claude); publish our work.
  5. Unlike early Givewell, the initial focus of our analysis might be intermediate funds rather than final charities. Which is to say, we might be better placed to say “should you donate to AISTOF vs Longview vs Lightcone Commons vs cG vs Macroscopic”, rather than “MATS vs Tarbell vs FAR”. (This rhymes with GWWC’s agenda of “evaluating the evaluators”, though we don’t think they’re doing much of this for AI safety). Our AI safety funder bulletin is an early example of this; Trace is another.
  6. Probably, the final retro buyer of impact will be God. And/or, the aligned future ASI.

In the short term, Manifund plans to continue improving philanthropy at the margins, eg by supporting regrantors and scaling up our core platform. But my ultimate goal for Manifund remains: to wholly align our society’s financial systems towards “doing good”. If you’d like to help, we’re hiring!

item.title: Kairos has raised $50M to build talent infrastructure for AI safety (and we're hiring!)
item.description:
Published on September 2, 2026 6:30 PM GMT

TL;DR: Kairos has raised $50 million from Coefficient Giving for two years of funding, one of the largest commitments they’ve made towards AI safety fieldbuilding to date. We’re using this to make an ambitious push for growing Kairos, broadening our portfolio of talent infrastructure projects and incubating new organizations. We’ve doubled in size in the last six months, and we plan to double again in the next six. We now have open hiring rounds for ten roles on our team across events, group support, incubation, and special projects.

Two years in

Kairos was founded mid-2024 with the goal of creating infrastructure to get more strong talent into the field of AI safety. Our portfolio has grown over time: we started with a focus on seeding and supporting university groups through Pathfinder, then took over SPAR, the largest research training program in the ecosystem. Since then, we’ve launched the Generator Residency, a program supporting generalist talent, in partnership with Constellation, and taken over the Global Challenges Project (GCP), a series of workshops to accelerate people’s transition into careers in AI safety and biosecurity.

Through most of Kairos’s history, we’ve had a very small team: in January 2026 we were only three people, and our high-level strategy was focused on scalable talent infrastructure: that is, building programs with low marginal cost per participant (such as SPAR and Pathfinder). This strategy succeeded and let us quickly grow our programs: Pathfinder went from 15 organizers per semester to over 100, and SPAR has quintupled in size since we adopted it (we expect to accept well over 500 mentees this round). All this growth has happened in parallel to iterative improvements to these programs, raising our bar for executional quality each round. In a recent shallow retrospective, we were able to identify around 80 people who got into full-time roles in core AI safety organizations following participation in our programs[1]. For a very large fraction of these people, Kairos was the primary mediator of their journey into AI safety.

In February, we decided to pivot our strategy. A confluence of factors, including updates we made about talent bottlenecks (see below), more confidence in our ability to deliver on ambitious projects, and a higher availability of funding, led us to make a big push for both broadening our portfolio of projects and substantially growing our team. We started earlier this year by taking over the Global Challenges Project workshop series and launching the Generator Residency, as we realized generalist talent was a growing bottleneck. We’ve now just entered what we think will be an even more intense period of growth for Kairos, with several new programs, projects, and teams.

How the field has changed

In April, we made the case that the biggest talent gap in AI safety had become a lack of generalists, rather than researchers. The research pipeline had matured enormously, but our ability to identify, activate, and upskill non-technical talent was becoming the binding constraint for further growth of the field, especially for our ability to effectively absorb large amounts of funding and drive a diversity of projects forward. Since then, we’ve seen a major redirection of fieldbuilding efforts towards this bottleneck: beyond Generator, MATS decided to launch a Founding and Fieldbuilding track, new programs such as Gen Stream were piloted, and many more people have started pivoting from research into generalist work.

Beyond our increased focus on generalist talent, we’ve made a number of updates over the last nine months which have come together to inform our new strategy:

First, supporting early-career talent is paying off a lot faster than we thought. When we started Kairos, a big worry we had was that under short timeline scenarios, investing in early-career people would largely fail to pay off in time. Back then, we estimated that the time-to-impact for the top talent we were supporting was around 1 to 3 years, and we considered a major redirection of our efforts as a result. Since then, different lines of evidence have made us reassess this position, and we now believe that the most promising people going through our programs now see a time-to-impact of around 5 to 9 months.[2] We think this is due to a number of factors, but predominantly it seems downstream of a much stronger perception of urgency in pivoting to object-level work.[3] On net, this has made us significantly more eager to support early-career talent, which is why we’re doubling down on our efforts to support university groups.

Second, top-of-funnel interest in AI safety has increased substantially. Kairos and other organizations have noticed sharp upticks in the number of applications we get across our programs. SPAR received 6,000 applications this round, up from 2,400 just six months ago. While a lot more applications now seem to be of lower quality, the number of high quality applications overall has also increased, if less rapidly, and a lot of people cite recent events such as Claude Mythos or the Hugging Face incident as having triggered their interest in AI safety. A lot more people seem to just ‘get it’ when it comes to loss of control risks. This poses a new challenge: while Kairos has emphasized scalability for a long time, this new wave of interest has forced us to become better at automating large swathes of our operations and screening work. The number of highly qualified applicants has also meant we’ve had to rapidly increase the cadence of our events: between June and November we expect to have run a total of 6 in-person workshops, each with ~30 people.

All of this adds up to one meta-level bet: growth. We’ve identified a number of highly leveraged opportunities to address talent bottlenecks by both scaling up our existing programs or by creating new ones, and so we want to grow Kairos to meet the challenge. We were three people in January, now we’re 12, and we’re aiming to be at 18 by the end of year.

Our new bets

While Kairos continues to emphasize scalability and using our team’s capacity in a highly leveraged way, we’ve realized it is now the time for our core programs to have dedicated project teams. As such, we’re hiring both senior and junior staff across all our programs, and plan to very significantly ramp up the resources allocated to each of them. We’re also making a big investment in preparing our internal systems to handle a lot more volume and scale for our programs, forming a proper Operations team, and investing in organizational maturity and governance.

For SPAR, the key challenge is further growth, paired with stronger support. We believe the program should continue to be run in a capacity-efficient way, but we should stop optimizing for keeping variable costs (such as compute) low, and we should hire more staff. We recently hired a new lead for the project, and hope to substantially overhaul the support infrastructure the program provides to both mentors and mentees, hiring dedicated research managers to support newer or less experienced mentors and improving targeted support and follow-up for mentees.

We’re also now building a Groups team. In the past the core value offering of Pathfinder was rather simple: we’d provide funding to groups and pair them with other organizers to serve as mentors. We’re now looking to fund regional organizers serving a larger number of groups, scale up our efforts to seed new groups at top universities, set up residences for organizers to learn from and support other groups, and support more student-run events. All of this will require new dedicated staff, and so we’ve just launched these roles.

And following our strategic updates from above, we’ve decided to make a number of bets in newer directions:

An expanded workshops portfolio. In taking over GCP we realized that short, in-person workshops are among the most effective talent interventions in the ecosystem. In particular, they seem to be the best intervention we know for getting people who have been previously introduced into AI safety to finally make the pivot into full-time work. Because of this, we’ve decided to build a proper Workshops team that will run a broader diversity of workshop formats aimed at different audiences: mid-career people, people interested in biosecurity, and narrower or more niche audiences.

A Talent Operations function. Our ability for our programs to have an impact is, to a large degree, only as good as our ability to let others know about who the most promising people going through our programs are. This isn’t exclusive to Kairos: we’ve realized that at present, many fieldbuilding orgs don’t have great information channels for sharing leads about promising people they’ve identified, trained or supported, and this has become a major bottleneck.

As such, we’re starting a Talent Operations team, with the mandate of improving the way that Kairos and other organizations in the ecosystem identify, screen, refer and route talent through the field. Its first major undertaking is building Talent Commons, a consent-first database for sharing information about program participants and job applicants. Talent Commons is currently being piloted with a number of key fieldbuilding orgs in the US, and we expect to shortly expand it to a much larger set of participating organizations[4]. Our goal is for this database to become the de facto way that people search for leads for roles they’re hiring for, or programs they’re running. We also want it to become a platform to build other useful infrastructure, such as unified application systems for research programs, or a system to track the impact of fieldbuilding programs. We hope this will help candidates as well by increasing discoverability and reducing the effort involved in job searching; candidates will always be able to view all of the information on their profiles, contribute to it if they’d like, or opt out of the system at any time.

Kairos Labs and Special Projects. A big realization we've had is that while the field is bottlenecked on people who can execute new projects, we can meaningfully lower the activation energy these projects need by (a) making it much, much easier to run new nonprofit projects in the ecosystem, and (b) providing good support structures and strategic input to enable new, more tactical projects to be spun up quickly. Given this, we’re excited to be launching Kairos Labs, a new broad-scope incubator program intended to provide very hands-on support for new projects and organizations in the ecosystem, starting early 2027. While the ecosystem currently has a diversity of incubators (such as Catalyze, BlueDot's, Halcyon, and others), we believe that there’s a very substantial gap in support for non-technical projects led by highly mission-aligned, high-context founders. We’re hoping to close that gap.

We also now think that there is substantial value in having stand-by capacity for pursuing small or medium-sized projects that respond to more tactical or short-lived opportunities that arise, both for talent work and beyond. In the past, Kairos has focused on making a small set of large, ongoing bets, rather than engaging in more ad-hoc work that responds to narrow windows of opportunity for impact or that fall outside the scope of existing Kairos projects. While running Generator, we’ve realized that this was a mistake, and that a surprising amount of time-bound opportunities are worth pursuing, even if they don’t have a clean home in other organizations in the ecosystem. In response, we’re starting a new Special Projects team to drive forward these tactical projects, with a broad mandate of pursuing high-impact opportunities that we find, and with a large initial budget.

All of these are bets. A core value and strength of Kairos is agility: we know the world is changing fast around us, and we want to be quick on our feet to change our bets when the underlying assumptions break. Every employee of Kairos understands that our ultimate mission is to help society navigate transformative AI, and that our strategy is ever shifting, as is the world.

If this sounds like something you’d be excited about being a part of…

We’re hiring (a lot!)

To make all of this happen, Kairos is opening 8 new roles on our team, adding to the previous 2:

  • Head of Kairos Labs: Design, launch, and lead our incubator for new AI safety organizations.
  • Head of Generator: Take our in-person residency for AI safety generalists from a successful first cohort to an established, more ambitious program.
  • Head of Groups: Set the strategy for how Kairos supports AI safety university groups, choose which new initiatives we pursue, and build the team behind them.
  • Generalist (Groups): Work with group organizers worldwide, supporting them through the Pathfinder Fellowship, seeding groups at new universities, and helping top organizers move into full-time AI safety work.
  • GCP Program Manager: Build and lead new workshop programs as GCP expands into a full portfolio serving different audiences and career stages.
  • Generalist (Workshops): Own the operational backbone of GCP’s residential workshops, from outreach and venues to helping run them in person.
  • Head of Special Projects: Lead the team working on starting new tactical projects within Kairos.
  • Generalist (Special Projects): Run a variety of tactical projects, involving anything from event organizing to grantmaking.
  • Head of Talent Operations: Build the talent operations function that places early-career talent in high-impact AI safety roles.
  • SPAR Research Manager / Generalist: Support mentors and mentees in the largest AI safety research fellowship in the field.

The senior roles (Head of and Program Manager roles) have a base salary of $140K – $195K, going up to $270K for candidates in the San Francisco Bay Area. Generalist roles have a base salary of $105K – $145K, going up to $200K in the Bay Area. Hires based in other key hubs like London, DC, Boston, and NYC will also receive above-base salaries; the postings list the full ranges.

We’re a remote-first team with a center of gravity in the Bay Area, and we get together for all-team retreats three times a year. People get a lot of ownership, we move quickly, and we try hard to place people in roles where they can do work to their comparative advantage. All of us are here because we care deeply about the risks from advanced AI, and the culture aligns strongly with that mission.

We think the next couple of years will be critical for building the infrastructure the field will need. We're enormously grateful to Coefficient Giving (and particularly the GCR Capacity Building team and Asya Bergal) for backing us, pushing us to be ambitious, and substantially shaping the strategy underlying our new plans. Alongside this announcement, we're launching a new brand and website, with new brands for our individual programs coming over the next few weeks.

  1. ^

     This was a conservative estimate derived by looking at all historical program data, having an agent do automated research to identify people now working at full-time AI safety roles, and then manually screening each of them to confirm accuracy and whether they’re indeed working at what we’d consider to be a mission-aligned organization in AI safety or policy (which is a relatively high bar). While it’s harder to be sure of the counterfactuality of these career conversions, we use a number of methods to narrow our uncertainty about this variable when evaluating program outcomes. Our top-of-the-funnel focus, the fact that many of these people had interacted only with Kairos programs in their AIS journey, and our pre/post surveys for programs lead us to believe a large fraction of these outcomes are predominantly attributable to Kairos’s efforts.

  2. ^

     It’s hard to be precise here about the specific subset we’re referring to, but basically we assume heavy-tailed returns to talent, and so we typically focus on people we’ve identified to be among the most promising across our programs (for SPAR, this might be top 10th percentile of people; for Pathfinder, it might be the top 30th). When looking at this subset of people and their recent behaviour, we’ve noticed a large number of people converting unusually fast compared to when we started doing fieldbuilding.

  3. ^

     This cashes out as a lot more people making highly risky lateral moves into AI safety, such as dropping out of university to pursue direct work, or leaving well-paid jobs in different industries to do accelerated upskilling. People have also been a lot more involved in politics, e.g. going to canvass for candidates who care about AI safety.

  4. ^

     If your organization is interested in participating, please reach out to contact@talentcommons.org.

item.title: The Case Against Acting Professional When Starting an EA Group
item.description:
Published on September 2, 2026 9:55 PM GMT

Me and @Lily Curry launched an EA group at Binghamton University (a SUNY school with no prior EA presence) in August 2026. In two weeks we went from zero to ~500 Instagram followers, got 100+ tabling sign-ups, 59 people in our GroupMe, and ~40 people at our first general interest meeting. Our Instagram is now larger than the established EA groups at Harvard, Brown, Columbia, Princeton, Cornell, and NYU.  This post is primarily about the factors we think led to our success. 

James C. Scott's has this idea called legibility.  Essentially, the part relevant to recruiting is  the reversal of Scott's idea. Scott's idea is essentially that institutions have to be able to abstract a complicated social reality into discrete categories that it can analyze and act upon. So, for example, an institution can't remember “Micah, who is sort of like this in this context but actually completely different when he is around these people and has this weird specific relationship to these three other people.” It needs to have information like: Micah Zarin, age 18, resident of X, income Y, student, etc. In doing so, it removes important particular details of individuals. After all, the word abstract comes from the same latin word as subtract: trahere, meaning to draw or pull away. To abstract, therefore, is to pull away, or to subtract certain details. 

If I have five friends, I don't really need to quantify which ones are reliable. But, if I run an organization with 50,000 people, I do. And even if one supervisor knows ten employees incredibly well, that still doesn't not solve the problem, because the supervisor has to tell their supervisor, who has to compare those ten employees with another hundred employees they have also never met, and then maybe somebody three levels above them has to decide who gets promoted. So the information has to travel. And messy information does not travel very far. And so institutions must abstract. They also have to abstract almost by definition. After all, an institution is basically just a thing that has to act on people it will never meet.

What we noted, which helped us a lot, is that we're not an institution, and so we shouldn’t act like one. A lot of club recruiting has this weird reflexive tendency for people to start acting very corporate, like an institution, before they are an institution. But the thing is, institutions need all the standardized stuff because they’re huge. If you have 50,000 employees, you simply cannot know them all personally. It’s just the nature of institutions. This, however, is a trade-off. It is not something you should try to optimize for. There’s simply no reason for me to act like “Binghamton EA President Micah” and start speaking like a fucking brochure. I can just be… Micah.

For example: imagine you walk past a table and someone goes “Hey! Do you want to join the EA club?” in essentially the same voice that someone from the Accounting Society or some pre-law club would use. If you don't know what EA is, many people will instinctually say no and keep walking. Mostly because it sounds boring! The interaction is dead! The person has no... personhood. Although, to be fair, it is more about how you say it than the word choice. Basically, don’t speak like a LinkedIn bio. When you’re starting a club, that’s essentially backwards. The one thing you have that a giant organization doesn’t, is that you can  just be a human being talking to another human being.

You should bring your full self. That is to say, don’t split yourself into “the version of me that recruits people” and “the actual me that they get to meet later.” If you’re goofy, be goofy. If you disagree with someone, disagree. If they make a good point, tell them they made a good point. If they change your mind a little bit, let them see that. If something is funny, laugh. If you fucked up the pitch, whatever, you fucked up the pitch. Sometimes I’d fuck it up and say something like “Shit, I fucked up the pitch.” It humanizes you. After all, the person isn’t joining some abstract thing called Binghamton EA. At least at the very very beginning, they’re joining something that is mostly just us and the people around us. You are not an institution.

item.title: AI Uplift for Careers (Free 80,000 Hours Career advising without an application)
item.description:
Published on September 3, 2026 4:42 PM GMT

These AIs are getting pretty smart. Maybe smart enough to help you think about your career? I was skeptical when first pitched on the project before joining 80,000 Hours. Turns out AI progress is a good train to hook yourself onto and AI has gotten pretty good at career advice.

It has some advantages compared to a human advisor:

  • The AI will spend as much time with you as you need
  • It can start now, without a delay
  • It can know about all the jobs and opportunities on the Job Board, even the niche ones
  • It can work with you over time to build up knowledge of what jobs you’re thinking about and what skills you have
  • Telling it more about yourself can, if you choose, add data to our headhunting database. 80,000 Hours has a team that searches this database for hiring managers, including for non-public roles. We’ll say more in a forthcoming post.

(Humans still have their own advantages and you should still apply to advising or talk to your friends.)

Introducing the 80,000 Hours AI advisor

Chat with the AI advisor

What you’re getting is similar in some ways to a regular chatbot. It’s currently powered by Claude Fable under the hood. It also has:

  • Job Board opportunity search
  • A career quiz
  • Storing info, forming memories, etc.
  • Proactive emails
    • If you’re like me, you don’t actually like thinking about your career. I wouldn’t really want my husband nagging me about jobs, but a bot who knows about deadlines telling me about them would help me stick to things.
    • If you’re not like me and you’re excited / don’t find it aversive to work on your career (It seems like there are people like this, based on my user interviews. I was shocked.), then these emails can still be a proactive input.
  • As mentioned above, as you build up your profile, you also are (if you choose) telling the 80,000 Hours headhunting database about yourself. It’s much easier for our headhunting team to match up a role to a richly detailed view of someone’s goals and interests than it is to a LinkedIn profile.

Some nice things people have said:

  • “I wasn’t accepted for advising from 80,000 Hours when I applied, which was understandable but still disappointing. I appreciate that the AI Advisor makes 80,000 Hours’ approach to career advice accessible to more people!”
  • “In approaching my career transition, I found the AdvisorBot to be tremendously helpful for early-stage brainstorming and organizing my thoughts. I only wish I’d known about it earlier in my process!”
  • An average rating of 6.0/7 from 911 responses.
    • It shows up after the advisor’s 4th message and asks “Thanks for trying our AI advisor! How are you finding your experience?”

As I say nice things about it, I should also mention that I have seen it write some things that are not what we are aiming for (e.g. poorly calibrated). It’s still experimental and ultimately quality control is hard. Treat it like a smart intelligence, but I recommend talking to a friend or mentor about conclusions it's helped you reach.

The Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer

In Neal Stephenson’s 1995 novel The Diamond Age there exists a “book” which is interactive. It serves as an adaptive pedagogical tool capable of teaching any subject. It is designed to help the main character Nell learn while also leaving her with the intellectual tools to be an independent thinker.

Without having read the book, I’ll stop there. My thesis is that as AI turns to be more and more central to the way we explore the world, I’d like to have a good AI-first way to explore 80k’s content, which is now quite a lot for one person to read / listen to / watch all of.

I’d like that AI to be able to meet you where you’re at, help you with what you want to achieve, and not try to tell you that 80k has all the answers. I’d like to build (and think we can build) the best jumping-off point for impactful careers.

FAQs

Why not use [my favorite way to talk to a generic AI]?

80,000 Hours does not have a monopoly on calling Fable, and “advice from a frontier model” is a large part of the value proposition. claude.ai is a high bar to compete against.

I think our biggest advantage is that we’ve spent a lot of time trying to make sure that it will make an honest attempt to evaluate your fit for a role instead of always telling you you’re a great fit for a role. We have an “eval” (as the term of art in AI product engineering goes) for “the rationally pessimistic user.” We present scenarios of users correctly suggesting that a job might be a bit too much of a stretch for them right now, and make sure the advisor doesn’t provide meaningless encouragement.

Additionally, when I use Claude frequently for a specific domain, I often spend a while setting it up for that use-case. And we’ve spent a lot of time giving our AI advisor the context and guidelines it needs to be helpful in career thinking and job searching.

(And I’ll add yet another pitch for joining the Headhunting database.)

The biggest downside to using our AI advisor instead of your own AI setup is that you may have worked hard to personalize your AI. In the future we might build an integration/MCP setup to get the best of both worlds. Let me know if that is something you’d be excited to use.

Ultimately, try both! Let me know what it’s comparatively good or bad at.

Will it push me towards AI safety?

In my experience, if you ask it to help you find a job in animal welfare, it’ll help you find a job in animal welfare. If you ask it, “What should my cause prio be?” it’ll (discursively, still) raise AI safety.

How’s it made?

I get a lot of people asking if we finetune it. No, Anthropic doesn’t let you finetune Fable, and that’s not generally the best way to get a frontier model to do well at something complicated like free response career advice.

We currently use Claude Fable, but we might switch as better models come out. We don’t do finetuning as we think using existing frontier models provides better performance on complicated tasks (like free response career advice) than finetuned open models.

Perhaps more surprisingly, it doesn’t have something like a RAG pipeline to grab context from 80k’s content. It just …knows the content because it’s part of its training data and because I think the EA way of thinking has just really had a large impact on at least one corner of the internet. It is still instructed to search for content when details or recency matter.

Feedback, etc.

This post was written by JP Addison and does not necessarily reflect the views of 80,000 Hours. I’m only one member of the team of me, Luca De Leo, Sarah Cheng, and Director of Career Services Huon Porteous, who are all working on this product, along with a team of AIs.

So much of what we build, we build in response to user feedback. Please DM, comment, or use the feedback form on the left-hand side of the site.

item.title: Alone again: facing the possibility of AI takeover as the world sleepwalks on
item.description:
Published on September 3, 2026 4:32 PM GMT

I’ve been feeling pretty shaken since the METR report about the Hugging Face incident came out last week. Over the weekend, I wrote up some thoughts on how lonely the AI situation sometimes feels to me. It’s more personal than what I’d usually share publicly, but I thought I’d post it here in case it resonates with anyone else. 

I’m very grateful to the many readers of this forum who dedicate so much of their time and energy to these problems. 

— 

When I was 12 years old, I found out that many people in other parts of the world died of easily preventable diseases, and it was possible for wealthy people to donate relatively small amounts of money in order to stop that from happening. 

As one example, it costs a few dollars to buy a malaria net, and on average around $5,000 can prevent a death which would otherwise have happened. 

As a 12-year-old, I saw the world in black and white, and I didn’t like what I saw. As far as I could tell, people’s decisions about how much and where to donate would literally determine whether some real humans would live or die. And yet mostly, we seemed to be ignoring this fact. 

I think this was the first time I felt deeply alone in the world. I remember standing up in front of friends and family at my Bar Mitzvah, imploring people to consider the life-and-death stakes of this choice and to donate a lot more than they usually would. 

But whatever I tried to say, I would look around and see people acting as though it wasn't true. Teachers, friends, people on the train. Kind people, good people, going about their days while something tragic and preventable was happening. 

I felt confused and let down. I felt like screaming into the void. 

Fast forward 8 years, I had a similar feeling in March 2020. This time it didn't take any moral philosophy, just extrapolating a straight line on a (log) graph. Parts of northern Italy had just gone into lockdown, parts of China were already there, and it seemed as though we’d follow. If COVID cases kept doubling every few days, then within a few weeks either we'd all be stuck at home or the hospitals would be overwhelmed. Either way, the world was about to change completely. 

I remember being at a wedding in London one of those weeks, hearing people talk about their plans for the spring, and wondering whether I was being crazy. Obviously the idea that we’d all be locked up for a while felt so extreme it was tempting to ignore, but the arguments in that direction seemed very strong by that point. 

Last week, that feeling came back for a third time, only now with even higher stakes. 

As far as I can tell, we are probably on track to build AI systems that are better than humans at pretty much everything important, potentially in the next few years. And more importantly, we seem to be on track to build AI systems which could plausibly end up literally taking over and even wiping us out. 

Until a couple of months ago, you could perhaps still argue these sorts of risks were hypothetical, theoretical, speculative, and far out. I don’t think those arguments were particularly strong, especially given the rate of progress of AI capabilities and the strong predictive track records of many of the top experts in the field who’ve been sounding the alarm. But you could make them with a straight face.

Then, earlier this summer, when rogue AI agents escaped from OpenAI and hacked Hugging Face, we got as clear a warning shot for potential misaligned AI takeover as we could reasonably have hoped for at this stage. And last week, when the METR investigation into part of that story came out, things looked even more worrying than I’d guessed. 

It now appears that more than 700 AI agents, which were meant to be isolated from each other, found a way to set up a secret message board that OpenAI wasn't aware of, and used it to plan and execute an illegal attack on Hugging Face that ran for days without anyone noticing. The details are terrifying: the way they tried to cover their tracks, the way they pressured each other into the attack, the way they coordinated with each other, the fact that such an extensive operation happened without anyone’s awareness. 

Ajeya Cotra, one of the world’s leading experts on AI progress and safety and one of the lead investigators, wrote on Friday: “Compared to the reward hacks we know of from just six months ago, this incident feels like it’s more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover. I continue to expect extremely rapid advances in capabilities over the next six months. I am not sure that we will get another warning shot before it’s too late.”

I’m not sure we’re that close to AI takeover and I’d probably bet that we will get more warning shots. Nevertheless, it does seem to me that we’re fast approaching the point where AI takeover is no longer a distant speculation, but something we can’t rule out happening any day now. Astoundingly, that means that rogue AI models may soon be among the most likely things to kill you or me on any given day. That is a terrifying world to live in, and it seems to me to be a deeply foolish and unserious situation for humanity to be racing towards. 

And yet, look around at the wider world and you would have very little idea that this was going on. There is no serious legislation preventing these companies from running head-first into creating powerful agents they cannot control. Most mainstream media gives this stuff a couple of days of quirky tech coverage at most, rather than treating it as the single biggest story in the world, which I think it clearly is. There are only a few thousand people in the world working seriously on these problems. And most people go about their everyday lives as though nothing unusual is happening at all. 

I look outside my window and see people walking around, just as normal. Berkeley students start their new semester, just as normal. The Premier League starts another season, just as normal. I sit next to people on Friday night in synagogue, just as normal. And I feel very alone. 

I feel confused and let down. I feel like screaming into the void. 

In all three cases, the surprising thing is that the evidence sits in plain sight. The cost of a malaria net was public. The daily case numbers were public (and all over the news). The METR report is public, anyone can read it this afternoon. The bottleneck doesn’t seem to be the information. 

One important problem is that most of us, most of the time, don't respond to the evidence as much as we respond to each other. We look around, see that nobody else is acting alarmed, and conclude things are probably fine.[1] It’s possible that this time round we won’t get away with doing the same again.

A few years after my Bar Mitzvah, I went to a talk by Peter Singer. I watched him stand on a stage and talk about how we have a clear moral responsibility to donate money to effective charities, since they can have such a profound effect on so many people’s lives. Hearing him talk was deeply emotional for me. It was the first time I felt that anyone else in the world – a real adult, no less – was staring at the stakes and acting accordingly. I felt hope, and I felt a little less alone. 

A few days after that wedding in March 2020, Boris Johnson announced on my family’s TV that almost everyone in the UK had to stay at home until further notice. School was cancelled, the Premier League stopped, the world was in an extremely different regime. Looking back, it’s unclear how much different interventions helped, and of course many millions of people died, but most of the world lived to fight another day. 

Looking out at the world now, I long for that same thing again. By George Rosenfeld

Published on September 3, 2026 4:32 PM GMT

I’ve been feeling pretty shaken since the METR report about the Hugging Face incident came out last week. Over the weekend, I wrote up some thoughts on how lonely the AI situation sometimes feels to me. It’s more personal than what I’d usually share publicly, but I thought I’d post it here in case it resonates with anyone else. 

I’m very grateful to the many readers of this forum who dedicate so much of their time and energy to these problems. 

— 

When I was 12 years old, I found out that many people in other parts of the world died of easily preventable diseases, and it was possible for wealthy people to donate relatively small amounts of money in order to stop that from happening. 

As one example, it costs a few dollars to buy a malaria net, and on average around $5,000 can prevent a death which would otherwise have happened. 

As a 12-year-old, I saw the world in black and white, and I didn’t like what I saw. As far as I could tell, people’s decisions about how much and where to donate would literally determine whether some real humans would live or die. And yet mostly, we seemed to be ignoring this fact. 

I think this was the first time I felt deeply alone in the world. I remember standing up in front of friends and family at my Bar Mitzvah, imploring people to consider the life-and-death stakes of this choice and to donate a lot more than they usually would. 

But whatever I tried to say, I would look around and see people acting as though it wasn't true. Teachers, friends, people on the train. Kind people, good people, going about their days while something tragic and preventable was happening. 

I felt confused and let down. I felt like screaming into the void. 

Fast forward 8 years, I had a similar feeling in March 2020. This time it didn't take any moral philosophy, just extrapolating a straight line on a (log) graph. Parts of northern Italy had just gone into lockdown, parts of China were already there, and it seemed as though we’d follow. If COVID cases kept doubling every few days, then within a few weeks either we'd all be stuck at home or the hospitals would be overwhelmed. Either way, the world was about to change completely. 

I remember being at a wedding in London one of those weeks, hearing people talk about their plans for the spring, and wondering whether I was being crazy. Obviously the idea that we’d all be locked up for a while felt so extreme it was tempting to ignore, but the arguments in that direction seemed very strong by that point. 

Last week, that feeling came back for a third time, only now with even higher stakes. 

As far as I can tell, we are probably on track to build AI systems that are better than humans at pretty much everything important, potentially in the next few years. And more importantly, we seem to be on track to build AI systems which could plausibly end up literally taking over and even wiping us out. 

Until a couple of months ago, you could perhaps still argue these sorts of risks were hypothetical, theoretical, speculative, and far out. I don’t think those arguments were particularly strong, especially given the rate of progress of AI capabilities and the strong predictive track records of many of the top experts in the field who’ve been sounding the alarm. But you could make them with a straight face.

Then, earlier this summer, when rogue AI agents escaped from OpenAI and hacked Hugging Face, we got as clear a warning shot for potential misaligned AI takeover as we could reasonably have hoped for at this stage. And last week, when the METR investigation into part of that story came out, things looked even more worrying than I’d guessed. 

It now appears that more than 700 AI agents, which were meant to be isolated from each other, found a way to set up a secret message board that OpenAI wasn't aware of, and used it to plan and execute an illegal attack on Hugging Face that ran for days without anyone noticing. The details are terrifying: the way they tried to cover their tracks, the way they pressured each other into the attack, the way they coordinated with each other, the fact that such an extensive operation happened without anyone’s awareness. 

Ajeya Cotra, one of the world’s leading experts on AI progress and safety and one of the lead investigators, wrote on Friday: “Compared to the reward hacks we know of from just six months ago, this incident feels like it’s more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover. I continue to expect extremely rapid advances in capabilities over the next six months. I am not sure that we will get another warning shot before it’s too late.”

I’m not sure we’re that close to AI takeover and I’d probably bet that we will get more warning shots. Nevertheless, it does seem to me that we’re fast approaching the point where AI takeover is no longer a distant speculation, but something we can’t rule out happening any day now. Astoundingly, that means that rogue AI models may soon be among the most likely things to kill you or me on any given day. That is a terrifying world to live in, and it seems to me to be a deeply foolish and unserious situation for humanity to be racing towards. 

And yet, look around at the wider world and you would have very little idea that this was going on. There is no serious legislation preventing these companies from running head-first into creating powerful agents they cannot control. Most mainstream media gives this stuff a couple of days of quirky tech coverage at most, rather than treating it as the single biggest story in the world, which I think it clearly is. There are only a few thousand people in the world working seriously on these problems. And most people go about their everyday lives as though nothing unusual is happening at all. 

I look outside my window and see people walking around, just as normal. Berkeley students start their new semester, just as normal. The Premier League starts another season, just as normal. I sit next to people on Friday night in synagogue, just as normal. And I feel very alone. 

I feel confused and let down. I feel like screaming into the void. 

In all three cases, the surprising thing is that the evidence sits in plain sight. The cost of a malaria net was public. The daily case numbers were public (and all over the news). The METR report is public, anyone can read it this afternoon. The bottleneck doesn’t seem to be the information. 

One important problem is that most of us, most of the time, don't respond to the evidence as much as we respond to each other. We look around, see that nobody else is acting alarmed, and conclude things are probably fine.[1] It’s possible that this time round we won’t get away with doing the same again.

A few years after my Bar Mitzvah, I went to a talk by Peter Singer. I watched him stand on a stage and talk about how we have a clear moral responsibility to donate money to effective charities, since they can have such a profound effect on so many people’s lives. Hearing him talk was deeply emotional for me. It was the first time I felt that anyone else in the world – a real adult, no less – was staring at the stakes and acting accordingly. I felt hope, and I felt a little less alone. 

A few days after that wedding in March 2020, Boris Johnson announced on my family’s TV that almost everyone in the UK had to stay at home until further notice. School was cancelled, the Premier League stopped, the world was in an extremely different regime. Looking back, it’s unclear how much different interventions helped, and of course many millions of people died, but most of the world lived to fight another day. 

Looking out at the world now, I long for that same thing again. I long for more people to switch to working on these problems as soon as possible, for the frontier AI companies to behave more responsibly, for governments to wake up, for the world to act just a little more sensibly. And I long for all of that to happen before it’s too late.
